_note: Spoken guide scripts, one per destination slug. The recorded ones live in media/audio/guide-<slug>.mp3; voice_guides.py records only what is missing, so this file is the queue and the archive at once. Keep each under about 90 seconds of speech, roughly 900 characters, and write for the ear: short sentences, one fact worth repeating, one instruction the traveller can act on.
pike-place-market: Pike Place Market. The oldest continuously running farmers market in the country, open since 1907. Come hungry: the fish throwers are the show, but the market is nine acres deep, with bakeries, noodle counters and the very first Starbucks. Go early for the flowers, stay for lunch, and keep an hour more than you planned.
the-met-museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Five thousand years of human making under one roof on Fifth Avenue. Nobody sees it all; pick two wings and walk them slowly. The Temple of Dendur, an actual Egyptian temple, sits in a hall of glass, and the rooftop in summer has a skyline view most visitors never find. Give it three hours and it will still be the fastest three hours of your trip.
staten-island-ferry: The Staten Island Ferry. Completely free, running all day and all night, and quietly one of the best boat rides in America. Twenty five minutes across the harbor, past the Statue of Liberty, with the whole downtown skyline stacked up behind you. Ride out, walk off, and take the next boat straight back. Stand on the right side going out; that is where the Statue is.
space-needle: The Space Needle. Built for the 1962 World's Fair and still the shape of the Seattle skyline. The upper deck is open air, and one level down the floor slowly rotates, and it is glass, all the way through, five hundred feet over the city. On a clear day you get Rainier to the south and the Olympics across the Sound. Sunset slots sell out first; book the hour before golden light.
bainbridge-island-ferry: The Bainbridge Island Ferry. Thirty five minutes across Puget Sound on a working state ferry, with the Seattle skyline shrinking behind you and the Olympic mountains ahead. Walk on, no reservation, and the fare is only collected leaving Seattle, so the ride home is free. On the island, Winslow's main street is ten minutes on foot from the dock: bookshops, bakeries, and a harbor full of sailboats.
lincoln-memorial: The Lincoln Memorial. Open all day and all night, free, and best at either end of the day. Climb the steps Martin Luther King spoke from and turn around: the Reflecting Pool, the Monument, and the Capitol line up in one straight mile. Then step inside and read the walls. The Gettysburg Address is carved to your left, and it is shorter than any speech you have ever sat through.
empire-state-building: The Empire State Building. Eighty six floors up, and it opened in 1931, built in just over a year while the country was falling apart. The open air deck is the one you came for; the higher 102nd floor is glassed in and quieter. Go early, before ten, or late, after nine, and skip the middle of the day entirely. And look down: the whole grid of Manhattan lays itself out beneath you like a drawing.
central-park: Central Park. Eight hundred and forty three acres, and every inch of it is man made, designed in 1858 and built out of swamp and rock. Enter at Bethesda Terrace for the fountain and the arcade, walk north into the Ramble to get pleasantly lost, and finish at Belvedere Castle for the view. Give it two hours. Give it a whole afternoon if the weather is kind.
brooklyn-bridge: The Brooklyn Bridge. Walk it from the Brooklyn side toward Manhattan; that is the direction where the skyline opens in front of you instead of behind. Finished in 1883, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, built with cables spun in place over the East River. The walk is about a mile, twenty five minutes at a stroll, and the pedestrian deck sits above the traffic. Early morning has the light and none of the crowd.
9-11-memorial-and-museum: The 9/11 Memorial. Two square voids, set exactly in the footprints of the towers, with water falling into them and disappearing into a second void below. Every name is cut into the bronze around the edges. The memorial outside is free and open; the museum below is a separate ticket and takes at least two hours. Take your time on the parapets. Some of the names have a white rose in them: that is somebody's birthday, placed there that morning.
grand-central-terminal: Grand Central Terminal. Look up first: the ceiling is a sky map with twenty five hundred stars, and it is painted backwards, as if you were looking down at the heavens from outside. Nobody has ever fully settled why. Then find the Whispering Gallery outside the Oyster Bar, stand facing a corner of the arch, and have someone stand at the opposite corner. Speak softly. They will hear you across the room.
the-high-line: The High Line. An abandoned elevated freight line that was going to be demolished, saved by two neighbors who went to a community meeting and found they were the only people in the room who wanted to keep it. Now it is a mile and a half of garden running thirty feet above the West Side. Walk it north from Gansevoort Street, and notice the planting: much of it is descended from the weeds that grew on the tracks while the line sat empty for twenty five years.
times-square: Times Square. It was Longacre Square until the New York Times moved in and put its name on the station in 1904. Everything you are looking at is legally required: the zoning here mandates a minimum amount of illuminated signage, so the lights are not excess, they are code. Come after dark, which is when it does what it does. Keep your wallet in a front pocket, and do not pay anyone in a costume.
chihuly-garden-and-glass: Chihuly Garden and Glass. Right at the foot of the Space Needle, and the best hour in Seattle Center. Eight galleries of blown glass, then a glass house with a hundred foot sculpture hanging overhead, then a garden where the glass grows among the real plants and you stop being sure which is which. Under an hour if you rush, and you should not rush.
gas-works-park: Gas Works Park. An abandoned gasification plant the city refused to tear down, so it kept the rusting towers and built a park around them. Climb the kite hill for the best skyline view in Seattle, with Lake Union and the seaplanes coming in below you. Sunset here is the local answer to the Space Needle, and it is free.
kerry-park-viewpoint: Kerry Park. It is barely a park, just a terrace on the side of Queen Anne hill, and it is the postcard: the Space Needle, downtown, Elliott Bay, and on a clear day Mount Rainier floating behind all of it. Five minutes to see, an hour if you wait for the light. Come at dusk when the city turns its lights on.
museum-of-pop-culture: The Museum of Pop Culture. The building is a Frank Gehry, and the story is that he cut up electric guitars and used the pieces as the model. Inside: Hendrix, Nirvana, science fiction, horror, and a tower built from six hundred instruments. Two hours, and it is the one museum in town where you are supposed to make noise.
seattle-aquarium: The Seattle Aquarium. Built right out over Elliott Bay on Pier 59, so the water under your feet is the same water in the tanks. The window on Puget Sound is the one to sit at: everything in it lives just outside. Ninety minutes, and check the feeding times when you walk in, because those are the fifteen minutes worth planning around.
starbucks-reserve-roastery: The Starbucks Reserve Roastery. Not the little store at Pike Place, this is the other one, fifteen thousand square feet of working roastery on Capitol Hill, with copper casks, coffee moving overhead through tubes, and a bar where they make things you cannot order anywhere else. Free to walk in, and worth it even if you do not drink coffee.
washington-monument: The Washington Monument. Five hundred and fifty five feet of marble, and if you look closely about a third of the way up, the stone changes color. Construction stopped for twenty three years when the money ran out and the Civil War came, and when they started again the original quarry was gone. The line in the stone is the war. Tickets to go up are a dollar and they go fast; the grounds are free and open all night.
jefferson-memorial: The Jefferson Memorial. Across the Tidal Basin, which is why most visitors look at it from a distance and never walk over. Do walk over. It is a domed rotunda open on every side, his words cut into the walls around the statue, and it is quieter than anything on the Mall. In late March and early April the cherry trees around the basin are the reason the whole city fills up.
lincoln-memorial-steps: The Lincoln Memorial steps. Find the engraving on the landing, about eighteen steps up: it marks the exact spot where Martin Luther King stood in August 1963. From there, the Reflecting Pool, the Washington Monument and the Capitol line up in a single straight mile, and that is the view a quarter of a million people were looking back from that day.
air-and-space-museum: The Air and Space Museum. The Wright Flyer, the Spirit of St. Louis, and the Apollo 11 command module are all in the same building, and it is free. Start upstairs and work down, because the crowd does the opposite. Two hours minimum. If you have a whole day and a car, the Udvar-Hazy annex out by Dulles has the Space Shuttle Discovery and an SR-71, and it is free too.
national-gallery-of-art: The National Gallery of Art. Free, always, and it holds the only Leonardo da Vinci painting in the Americas, a portrait called Ginevra de' Benci, in the West Building. The two buildings are joined by an underground concourse with a moving walkway under a ceiling of light, which is worth the trip by itself. Two hours in one building; do not try to do both.
arlington-national-cemetery: Arlington National Cemetery. Four hundred thousand graves, and it began as an act of spite: the land was Robert E. Lee's estate, and the Union started burying its dead in his wife's rose garden. Walk up to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier for the changing of the guard, on the hour in winter, every half hour in summer. It is guarded every minute of every day, and has been since 1937.
